title: Mark Strizic: the career of an Australian photographer

paragraphs.text: Photographer Mark Strizic was one of an important group of European artists who immeasurably enriched Australia in the latter half of the 20th century. But Strizic was a bit different. After arriving in the Australian city of Melbourne in 1950, he embarked on a 50-year career which was much more complex and diverse than that of any of the other immigrant photographers. He not only worked in many different photographic styles, but was also interested in new and experimental photographic techniques, as well as book design and production, and tertiary teaching.

Artistic collaboration was fundamental to Strizic's career. In 1960 Strizic worked with architectural critics and historians to produce a picture book called 'Melbourne: A Portrait', which is a charming object even today. Unusually for a book of the period, the entire publication was printed using a new printing process which integrated text and images, rather than the photographs being printed from plates engraved separately to the letterpress text. As the book's designer, Strizic was able to freely move the rectangular photographs up and down or across the square pages so that the composition of one page visually coordinated with the next. Expansive fields of blank paper, which sometimes also included floating lines of text, brought each consecutive double-page spread together into a graphic composition which was visually related to the subject matter of the photographs.

Although modestly scaled and priced, the book did not lack ambition. The text was translated into Italian and German, anticipating international interest in the images of cosmopolitan Melbourne. Strizic himself acknowledged that its inspiration came from a publication by his father, an architect, about his own hometown in Europe. It was clearly to this more reflective European style of 'city book' that Strizic aspired, rather than to the superficial commercialism of other Australian photo books of the time - although both cast Melbourne in a positive light. 'Melbourne: A Portrait' won a Book of the Year Award in 1961, and the award duly recognised the integrated design of the complete book package.

In 1967 and 1968, Strizic worked on two important projects with Sun Books. This publishing company was experimenting with different ways of taking advantage of the boom in paperback publishing that was bringing book prices down and increasing the popular market for a diverse range of formats and subjects. In what he realised was a risky move professionally, Strizic was involved in one project as a stills photographer on the pioneering film '2000 Weeks'. He turned the stills into a cheap paperback book to accompany the film, with each page tightly packed with his photographs and dialogue from the film.

Strizic worked with Sun Books again on a high-end, limited-edition book called 'Involvement'. The idea was that Strizic would collaborate with Clifton Pugh, a well-known Australian painter, taking photographs of people Pugh had painted over the years, and which Pugh chose to include in the book. Painting and photograph would be shown side by side. The book was not designed by Strizic himself, as had been the case with 'Melbourne: A Portrait', but by a designer whose out-of-balance juxtaposition of the large colour plates with Strizic's black-and-white photographs gave each double-page spread a cluttered feel. This, combined with the book's pretentious leather binding and grandiose text, makes for a curiously unsatisfying package. Despite this, Strizic's portraits in the book are fine examples of his developing photographic style. He shot his models against dominating backgrounds and with intruding out-of-focus foreground elements. This had the effect of amplifying their personalities; they appear to be strongly asserting themselves against their environment. In 1968, this set of photographs was exhibited as 'Some Australian Personalities' at the National Gallery of Victoria in its first one-person photography show, and was critically acclaimed.

A final important collaboration was with the architect and cultural critic Robin Boyd. In 1970 Strizic photographed and designed Boyd's book 'Living in Australia'. In it Boyd put forward his own design philosophy to counter the ugliness which both he and Strizic saw as enveloping Australia. Strizic's graphically compelling photography, in which the exposed wooden beams and large picture windows of Boyd's domestic architecture are shot in deeply penetrating diagonal focus, reinforces the larger social message of the book. The publication has recently been successfully repackaged and republished with additional photography, and it remains a classic in Australian design publishing.

Unlike many of his fellow photographers who established their careers in the 1960s, Strizic sustained a busy practice as an exhibiting artist, both solo and in collaboration, at key commercial galleries. Another difference was that he spent a long period teaching in the new photography departments which were starting up in Melbourne art schools and technical colleges as part of the 1970s photography boom. In 1988 he returned to his early negatives of Melbourne streets for a final exhibition. Since then he has gradually become well known as a nostalgic photographer of 'old Melbourne', 'disappearing Melbourne', or 'marvellous Melbourne'. But, seen in its entirety, his career is much more complex than that. Through his constant experimentation, and his long-term engagement on many levels with a range of artists and designers, he played an important, if under-the-radar role in much that was new, innovative, and important in Australian culture.

The accompanying photography was inadequate.
